name: Explosion
desc: Server notifies the client of an explosion (TNT, creeper, bed in Nether/End, etc).

fields.name: motionX/Y/Z
fields.desc: Player knockback velocity from the explosion

notes: Affected blocks are sent as byte triplets (x, y, z) relative to the explosion center. The client applies particle effects and knockback to the local player.

writeup.p: S27 is the server's explosion broadcast: center x/y/z floats, strength, a list of affected block positions encoded as byte triplets relative to the center, and a per-player knockback vector as three floats. WorldServer sends one S27 per affected player (corpus line 901), with the knockback floats computed per player from the explosion's player knockback map. The client both renders the destroyed blocks and applies the knockback vector to the local player, which is why it is the second half of every velocity module's packet filter alongside S12PacketEntityVelocity.

NetHandlerPlayClient.handleExplosion builds an Explosion object from the center and strength, calls doExplosionB(true) to spawn particles and sounds, then adds the packet's motion floats straight into thePlayer.motionX/Y/Z. Critically, the knockback is applied unconditionally on the main thread; there is no entity-ID check because the packet is per-player. That makes S27 the standard fallback for anti-cheat velocity implementations: servers that hide S12 knockback in explosion packets still deliver S27, so clients must filter both.

S27 is the most-touched clientbound packet in this batch. Every velocity module in the corpus filters it: Memeware and Nekoware cancel it in a shared combat/Velocity pattern, Rise 5.99's Velocity scales or cancels it, Sigma's AntiVelocity handles it in basic mode, Spicy's AntiKnockback cancels it, and Tenacity's VelocityModule scales it by the same horizontal/vertical settings as S12. Rise 6.x splits this into a suite of per-server modes (Standard, Vulcan, Redesky, UniversoCraft, BufferAbuse), all of which touch S27. Movement modules also consume it: Rise 5.99's Fly (Minemenclub) and LongJump (Hycraft, Vulcan) cancel S27 to control knockback timing, and Sigma's Fly uses it for explosion-based boosting.

The exploit surface is bidirectional. Client-side, scaling or cancelling the knockback floats is invisible to the server because S27 is one-way; anti-cheats can only infer from resulting motion, which is why velocity modules keep the S12 and S27 paths symmetric. Server-side, a hostile server can send S27 with huge motion floats (Rise's ExplosionCheck guards against motion >= Byte.MAX_VALUE) or enormous affected-block lists to stall the client's block-position loop, which is exactly the flood Tenacity's AntiExploit rate-limits. Rise's ItemDamageComponent also counts S27 as a damage source to resync the player's health model.

implementation.overview: The explosion broadcast that carries both destroyed-block positions and a per-player knockback vector. Every velocity module in the corpus filters it alongside S12PacketEntityVelocity; Rise 6.x dedicates five per-server modes to it, movement modules cancel it to shape knockback, and Tenacity's AntiExploit rate-limits it against crash floods. The packet is one-way, so all client abuse is invisible to the server.
implementation.server_handling: WorldServer.createExplosion computes the affected block list and a per-player knockback Vec3 from the blast, then sends a dedicated S27 to each EntityPlayerMP (corpus line 901). The knockback map is filled only for players the explosion actually hits, so players outside the blast receive an S27 with zero motion floats but still get the visual. No client acknowledgement and no rate limiting in vanilla.
implementation.protocol_notes: Wire format: three floats (center), float strength, int record count, then count byte triplets as offsets from the center (each block position is center + signed byte), then three floats of player motion. The triplet encoding caps the block list extent at 127 blocks from the center, which is why ExplosionCheck thresholds at Byte.MAX_VALUE. PLAY state only.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: Anti-cheats cannot see the mutation, so they infer velocity removal from motion deltas: after a flagged hit they compare the player's acceleration against the expected knockback curve. That is why legit-looking modes exist: Tenacity's horizontal/vertical percentages, Rise 6.x's per-server modes, and movement modules that cancel S27 only while airborne. The Rise 6.x BufferAbuse and PingSpoofComponent keep the S27 path consistent with transaction buffering, since a desynced knockback stream is a strong velocity flag on Vulcan and Watchdog.

modules.name: Velocity / AntiKnockback
modules.purpose: Cancel or scale explosion knockback so hits from TNT, creepers and beds apply reduced or zero motion.
modules.how_it_works: PacketReceiveEvent filter: if the packet is S27PacketExplosion, either cancel it outright or multiply motionX/Y/Z by horizontal/vertical percentage settings before the vanilla handler applies them. Tenacity scales in place; Memeware/Nekoware/Spicy cancel; Rise 5.99 and Sigma switch behavior per configured mode.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: In-place scaling is safer than cancel: the server still sees a packet pass and the client motion delta stays consistent with a legitimately weaker explosion. Full cancel flags on anti-cheats that measure knockback absence, which is why modes like Rise's Minemenclub variants only zero S27 while airborne.
modules.variations: Memeware and Nekoware cancel S27 in combat/Velocity. Rise 5.99 scales per mode (Cancel/Push/etc.). Sigma AntiVelocity handles S27 in basic mode only. Spicy AntiKnockback cancels it. All six clients pair the S27 filter with the S12PacketEntityVelocity filter in the same handler.

modules.name: StandardVelocity / VulcanVelocity / RedeskyVelocity / UniversoCraftVelocity / BufferAbuseVelocity
modules.purpose: Per-server velocity modes that each define their own S27 (and S12) handling, from full cancel to percentage scaling to transaction-buffered removal.
modules.how_it_works: Each mode is a Rise Mode<Velocity> subclass with an @EventLink PacketReceiveEvent listener. StandardVelocity scales or cancels S27 based on horizontal/vertical sliders and an Explosion Ignore boolean. VulcanVelocity, RedeskyVelocity and UniversoCraftVelocity cancel or mutate S27 to match each server's knockback checks. BufferAbuseVelocity folds S27 into the client's transaction-buffer manipulation so the knockback stream stays consistent while transactions are delayed.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: The per-server split exists because each anti-cheat (Vulcan, Redesky, UniversoCraft, etc.) measures knockback differently. Percentage modes are low-risk; full-cancel modes only run when the server's velocity check is known to be weak, and BufferAbuse keeps S27 consistent with the buffered transaction stream so the two cannot be cross-correlated.
modules.variations: The same five modes exist in Rise 6.1.30 and 6.2.4 with near-identical bodies; 6.2.4 adds WatchdogPredictionVelocity and Grim-family modes that do not reference S27. PingSpoofComponent in both versions lists S27PacketExplosion in the velocity packet class set it buffers, and ItemDamageComponent counts S27 as a damage input.

modules.name: Fly / LongJump
modules.purpose: Cancel explosion knockback inside movement exploits so a mid-air boost or long jump is not interrupted by server-applied velocity.
modules.how_it_works: Rise 5.99's LongJump cancels S27 (and S12) in onPacketReceive when the Hycraft or Vulcan mode is active; its Fly cancels S27 in the Minemenclub mode. Sigma's Fly treats S27 as a velocity source for explosion-boost movement. The cancel keeps the server's knockback from perturbing the carefully staged motion values the module computes each tick.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Cancelling S27 mid-jump is one of the oldest velocity tells because the motion discontinuity is measurable. These modes rely on the server's knockback check being absent or on the jump's speed exceeding what the anti-cheat expects, which is why they are mode-gated to specific servers.
modules.variations: Rise 5.99 Fly handles S27 in Minemenclub mode; Sigma Fly uses S27 as an explosion boost input in its packet handler; Sigma's InfiniteAura imports S27 (the corpus shows the import only, unused in the visible body).

modules.name: AntiExploit
modules.purpose: Block crash-exploit S27 floods from malicious servers by bounding explosion strength and arrival rate.
modules.how_it_works: PacketReceiveEvent handler: cancels S27 when abs(strength) > 1 or when two explosions arrive within 1 ms, printing a blocked-exploit chat message. The same handler covers resource-pack, camera, particle and teleport crash vectors with the same pattern, and a separate packet-count throttle kicks the client-side watchdog when inbound packet rate exceeds 100/sec.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Not a cheat at all, it is client-side self-defense against lag machines. Nothing flags it because it only cancels inbound packets. Its strength heuristic is coarser than Rise's ExplosionCheck, which thresholds the motion floats at Byte.MAX_VALUE instead of the strength float.
modules.variations: Rise 6.1.30/6.2.4 ship the equivalent as a security feature, ExplosionCheck.java, which cancels S27 when any motion float exceeds Byte.MAX_VALUE (mirroring the wire format's signed-byte block offsets).

modules.name: Debugger
modules.purpose: Print explosion velocity values to chat as part of a packet-level debug overlay for development and bypass work.
modules.how_it_works: PacketReceiveEvent handler: when the Velocity toggle is on and the packet is S27PacketExplosion, prints DeltaX/DeltaY/DeltaZ from func_149149_c / func_149144_d / func_149147_e, the same motion floats velocity modules mutate. The debug output shows the exact knockback vector a server sends, letting a developer tune a velocity mode's scaling against real traffic.
modules.anti_cheat_notes: Read-only; prints to chat only. It exists to make the velocity suite's tuning data visible, and it is the only module in the corpus that reads S27 without mutating or cancelling it.
modules.variations: Identical in Rise 6.1.30 and 6.2.4. Rise 5.99 has a PacketDebugger module for the same role, but the corpus shows no S27 reference in it.

implementation.general_hooks: PacketReceiveEvent is the universal hook: every S27 consumer in the corpus registers on the receive path before the vanilla handler applies the knockback.
implementation.client_variations: Classic clients mutate or cancel the packet object inside the event. Rise 5.99/6.x call event.setPacket / event.setCancelled on their own event bus. Tenacity and Spicy use IEventListener-style lambda handlers. Rise 6.x additionally routes S27 through components (ItemDamageComponent, PingSpoofComponent) and a security layer (ExplosionCheck) in addition to modules.
